text: Measure Summary Measure Title Duct Sealing and Insulation Measure This upgrade measure involves sealing HVAC ducts and adding insulation in Definition applicable dwelling units. After the upgrade, the units will achieve 5% duct leakage to the outside and an R-8 duct insulation level. Applicability This measure applies to all dwellings with ductwork located in unconditioned space that have one or both of the following characteristics: • More than 6% duct leakage to the outside • Less than R-6 duct insulation. With these applicability constraints, the measure upgrade applies to about 46% of the existing dwelling units. Not Applicable This measure does not apply to dwelling units with any of the following characteristics: • 6% (or less) duct leakage to the outside and R-6 (or greater) duct insulation • 0% leakage to the outside. These constraints exclude 54% of the dwelling units from receiving this measure upgrade. File(s) 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Technology Summary Ducts are used to distribute conditioned air throughout a house from a forced-air heating or cooling system, such as a central furnace, central air conditioner, or ducted heat pump. This measure applies duct sealing to all homes that use ducts for air distribution. Sealing ductwork located in unconditioned spaces saves energy, improves thermal comfort, and can even improve indoor air quality by patching return leaks on ducts exposed to pollutants. This increases the efficiency and performance of HVAC systems, allowing conditioned air to be distributed more effectively to where it is needed while keeping it clean and separated from dusty areas. 1.1 Introduction to Technology It is estimated that 20%–30% of air moving through ducts leaks into unconditioned spaces instead of reaching its intended destination in the home (ENERGY STAR, 2025). This leakage reduces the efficiency of the heating and cooling system. Duct sealing and insulation reduce heat loss through ductwork and the loss of conditioned air to unconditioned spaces, thereby reducing the amount of input energy needed to deliver the desired amount of heating or cooling. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE, 2011), many homes have HVAC ducts located in unconditioned spaces like attics or crawl spaces. For ducts located in conditioned spaces, duct sealing and insulation will have little impact on energy use. Ductwork is often hidden in walls, ceilings, attics, basements, or crawlspaces, which can make repairs challenging. However, there are several ways to reduce leakage and improve efficiency. Duct sealing can reduce leakage directly and can be achieved by several actions (ENERGY STAR, 2025): (1) repair damaged or disconnected ducts and straighten out flexible ducts that are tangled or crushed; (2) seal all leaks and connections with mastic, UL-Listed tape, or an aerosol- based sealant; (3) seal all duct boots to the drywall or subfloor; (4) include a new filter as part of any duct system improvement; (5) install a filter slot opening cover where missing or where the existing cover does not provide an adequate seal.
